The aerobic degradation performance of wastewater was evaluated in the long-term batch mode. 1 L of CGW and other effluents were added to the beaker, respectively, followed by the actual aerobic tank sludge (5 g/L). The DO of system was 3~4 mg/L, and the gas volume was controlled by the flowmeter. Each period was divided into aeration (36 h), sedimentation (2 h) and drainage (0.5 h), and the wastewater was supplemented to 2 L to restart the next period. The COD of water samples during different periods was determined after filtration.

The CGW degradation performance of anaerobic sludge was also evaluated in a long-term batch mode at different DO concentrations. 1 L of CGW and 6 g/L of domesticated anaerobic sludge were added to the open reagent bottle (2.5 L), and then placed in a thermostatic shaker at 35 °C and 100 rpm. Gas flow was regulated by a flow meter, and DO levels (0-0.1, 0.1-0.2, 0.2-0.3, 0.3-0.5, 0.5-0.8, and 0.8-1 mg/L) were monitored and adjusted every 3-4 h using a DO meter (HQ30d, Hach, USA). The HRT was maintained at 36 h. The supernatant was taken every 2 d and filtered through the membrane (0.45 μm) for the detection of COD and BOD5.

OUR test adopted aerobic sludge sourced from a municipal WWTP, which was washed 3-4 times with distilled water before use. The total volume of test was 20 mL. The test group comprised 8 mL of sludge (4 g/L), 10 mL of water sample, 1 mL of nutrient medium (as detailed in the Table S2) and 1 mL of deionized water. In contrast, the control group contained 8 mL of sludge (4 g/L), 1 mL of nutrient matrix and 11 mL of deionized water. Initially, the water samples were vigorously agitated in a high-speed magnetic stirrer for 1-2 h until DO achieved saturation. Furthermore, the deionized water, sludge, and nutrient medium were rapidly blended and aerated for 30 min until DO reached saturation. It is noteworthy that the DO concentration was monitored at 10 s intervals until it descended below 0.5 mg/L. Prior to the sample assessment, 3,5-dichlorophenol was employed as a standard toxin (EC50: 2-25 mg/L) to ascertain the sensitivity of sludge. The method of testing for heterotrophic bacteria OUR is the same as that for total OUR, and 1 mL ATU (232 mg/L of propylene sulfur) was added to the experimental group before testing. Subsequently, nitrifying bacteria OUR was calculated as the difference between total OUR and heterotrophic bacteria OUR (Hei et al. 2022).

The mixture for testing nitrification rate was composed of nutrient medium, sludge and water samples, and distilled water was added to make up the volume to 100 mL. The remaining components are mixed first and then the activated sludge inoculum is added. During the microbial incubation process, the microorganisms in the activated sludge in the incubator ensure full contact with CGW. The incubator temperature was controlled at 22±2 °C and the incubation time was 4 h. Subsequently, the conical flask was removed from the incubator and the sealing film was detached, and a certain volume of mixed liquid was extracted with a sealed syringe, and finally the liquid was filtered by an aqueous polyethersulfone needle filter (Zhu et al. 2023). Firstly, 0.05 mL of sludge from the reactor during stage III was taken and washed three times using PBS solution. Then, live/dead cells of the sludge were fluorescently stained with a staining kit (Beijing Solarbio Science & Technology Co., Ltd., China). And the kit contained two solutions, calcein and propidium iodide (PI), for staining live (Ex=490 nm, Em=515 nm) and dead (Ex=535 nm, Em=617 nm) cells, respectively. Both calcein and PI can be excitable by light at 490 nm, thus laser scanning confocal microscope (LSCM, LEXT OLS5100, OLYMPUS, Japan) could be used to monitor both live and dead cells. Finally, the color of dead and live cells in the stained sludge was observed to be red and green, respectively, by LCSM at an emission wavelength of 505-620 nm, an excitation wavelength of 490 nm, and an exposure time of 4-10 us/pixel. Based on the distribution of colors, the number of live and dead cells could be observed to determine the activity of the sludge.

The supernatant was removed from the sludge mixture by centrifugation at 5000 r/min and washed three times with 0.1 M PBS. The sludge was then sonicated (200 W) at 4 °C for 30 min and broken up, followed by centrifugation at 20000 r/min, and the resulting supernatant is the crude enzyme solution. 0.2 mM NADPH, 1 mM FAD, 0.8 mM EDTA, 40 mM PBS and 50 µL crude enzyme solution were added sequentially to an enzyme plate. FAD acts as a coenzyme for phenol hydroxylase which hydroxylates phenol to catechol, and NADPH provides the H+ required for hydroxylation, thus the absorbance of NADPH at 340 nm can be measured by using a microplate reader to characterize the activity of phenol hydroxylase (Zhang et al. 2022). First, 0.3 mL crude enzyme solution (as tested for phenol hydroxylase) and 2 mL catechol (0.1 M) were added to the centrifuge tube, respectively, and then the absorbance at 375 nm was immediately measured using a microplate reader. As catechol is cleaved to yellow 2-hydroxymuconic acid by the action of catechol dioxygenase, a specific absorption peak occurs at 375nm, so the variation in absorbance can characterize the activity of catechol dioxygenase. High-throughput sequencing was utilized to determine the microbial community structure of sludge samples during stage III. The operation process of microbial Community analysis was based on the references (Song et al. 2019, Tian et al. 2020). Firstly, DNA in sludge samples was extracted using the Mag-Bind® Soil DNA Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instruction. The 16srRNA gene of the V3-V4 target region was amplified by PCR with preprimer 341F (CCTACGGGGNGGCWGCAG) and reverse primer 805R (GACTACHVGGGGTATCTAATCC). All polymerase chain reaction mixtures were purified using the MinElute Gel Extraction Kit (Qiagen, Germany). Then, the PCR-amplified products were purified and quantified by SanPrep DNA Gel Extraction Kit (Sangong Bio, China) and Qubit 3.0 DNA Detection Kit (Life, USA), respectively. Finally, the PCR products were adjusted to equalize their DNA concentrations and then sequenced on the Miseq sequencing platform (Illumina, USA). Analysis of 16S rRNA gene sequences was conducted according to previous method (Wang et al. 2011).

DNA extraction and PCR amplification methods were performed in the same way as for the microbial community structure tests. Metagenomic sequencing was conducted using the Illumina NovaSeq sequencing platform (Shanghai Meiji Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd., China). Firstly, the optimized sequences were assembled by splicing using the assembler software (MEGAHIT, https://github.com/voutcn/megahit, version 1.1.2) based on the principle of succinct de Bruijn graphs (Li et al. 2015). Among the splicing results, contigs larger than 300 bp were screened as the final assembly results. ORF prediction of contigs from the splicing results was subsequently performed using Prodigal/MetaGene (http://metagene.cb.k.u-tokyo.ac.jp/) (Noguchi et al. 2006). Genes with nucleic acid lengths greater than 100 bp were selected and translated into amino acid sequences. In the construction of non-redundant gene set, the gene sequences predicted from all samples were clustered (parameters: 90% identity, 90% coverage) using CD-HIT (http://www.bioinformatics.org/cd-hit/, version 4.6.1) (Fu et al. 2012), and the longest gene in each class was taken as the representative sequence to construct the non-redundant gene set.

High-quality reads from each sample were individually compared to the non-redundant gene set (95% identity) using SOAPaligner software (http://soap.genomics.org.cn/, version 2.21) (Li et al. 2008) to statistically characterize the abundance information of genes in the corresponding samples. Diamond (http://www.diamondsearch.org/index.php, version 0.8.35) (Buchfink et al. 2015) was utilized to align amino acid sequences with the NR database (BLASTP with an e-value of 1eˉ5). Simultaneously, employing the taxonomic information database within the NR repository, we acquired species annotations. Ultimately, species abundance was computed by summing the gene abundances corresponding to the respective species. Additionally, Diamond was employed to align amino acid sequences with the KEGG database (BLASTP with an e-value of 1eˉ5), providing the KEGG functions associated with the respective genes. The abundances of functional categories were calculated by summing the abundances of genes corresponding to KO, Pathway, EC, and Module.
